questiontext.text: The LLM test-generation pipeline (Meta's ACH flow, FSE 2025) chains three agents. In what order do they run?

answer.text: Mutation agent → Equivalence agent → Test agent

feedback.text: Correct — mutants are generated, screened for equivalence, then the survivors are targeted by generated tests.

answer.text: Test agent → Mutation agent → Equivalence agent

feedback.text: Tests are written last, to kill the non-equivalent mutants that survive screening.

answer.text: Equivalence agent → Mutation agent → Test agent

feedback.text: There is nothing to judge for equivalence until the mutation agent has produced mutants.

answer.text: Mutation agent → Test agent → Equivalence agent

feedback.text: Equivalence screening happens before test generation, so the test agent is not asked to kill uncatchable mutants.

generalfeedback.text: The pipeline is a three-agent flow in the order Mutation → Equivalence → Test: the mutation agent seeds faults, the equivalence agent filters out uncatchable (equivalent) mutants, and the test agent generates tests that kill the remaining non-equivalent mutants.

questiontext.text: What is the job of Agent 1, the mutation agent?

answer.text: Generate mutants that target specific fault classes

feedback.text: Correct — the mutation agent seeds faults aimed at particular fault classes.

answer.text: Decide whether a mutant is equivalent

feedback.text: That is the equivalence agent's job (Agent 2).

answer.text: Write a test that kills a mutant

feedback.text: That is the test agent's job (Agent 3).

answer.text: Run the CI pipeline and reject flaky tests

feedback.text: Flakiness is a quality gate on the test agent's output, not the mutation agent's role.

generalfeedback.text: The mutation agent (Agent 1) generates mutants, deliberately targeting specific fault classes rather than making blind syntactic tweaks.

questiontext.text: What is the job of Agent 2, the equivalence agent?

answer.text: Decide whether a mutant is equivalent (uncatchable) to the original

feedback.text: Correct — it acts as an LLM-as-judge, filtering out mutants no test could ever kill.

answer.text: Generate the mutants in the first place

feedback.text: Generating mutants is the mutation agent's role (Agent 1).

answer.text: Generate a test that kills the mutant

feedback.text: Writing the killing test is the test agent's role (Agent 3).

answer.text: Measure the code coverage of the resulting suite

feedback.text: The equivalence agent judges equivalence; it does not compute coverage.

generalfeedback.text: The equivalence agent (Agent 2) is an LLM-as-judge that decides whether a mutant is equivalent — semantically identical to the original and therefore impossible for any test to kill — so those mutants are removed before the test agent runs.

questiontext.text: What is the job of Agent 3, the test agent?

answer.text: Generate a test that kills the non-equivalent mutant

feedback.text: Correct — the test agent writes a test whose result distinguishes the mutant from the original.

answer.text: Generate the mutants

feedback.text: That is the mutation agent (Agent 1).

answer.text: Judge whether the mutant is equivalent

feedback.text: That is the equivalence agent (Agent 2).

answer.text: Strip comments from the source before judging

feedback.text: Comment stripping is a preprocessing step for the equivalence agent, not the test agent's job.

generalfeedback.text: The test agent (Agent 3) generates a test that kills the mutant — a test that produces a different result on the mutant than on the original — for the mutants the equivalence agent judged non-equivalent.

questiontext.text: In this pipeline, what does it mean for a test to kill a mutant?

answer.text: The test produces a different result on the mutant than on the original program

feedback.text: Correct — an observable difference between mutant and original is what kills it.

answer.text: The test passes on both the mutant and the original

feedback.text: If a test passes on both, it fails to distinguish them and does not kill the mutant.

answer.text: The mutant is deleted from the source tree

feedback.text: Killing is about detection by a test, not about removing the mutant from disk.

answer.text: The equivalence agent labels the mutant as equivalent

feedback.text: A mutant labelled equivalent is precisely the one that can never be killed.

generalfeedback.text: A test kills a mutant when it yields a different, observable result on the mutant than on the original program. The whole point of the test agent is to generate such mutation-killing tests.

name.text: What an equivalent mutant is here

questiontext.text: In this pipeline, an equivalent mutant is one that:

answer.text: Behaves identically to the original, so no test can ever kill it (uncatchable)

feedback.text: Correct — that is why the equivalence agent filters it out before the test agent runs.

answer.text: Is killed by every test the test agent generates

feedback.text: That describes an easily-killed mutant, the opposite of an equivalent one.

answer.text: Fails to compile and is discarded by the build

feedback.text: That is invalid code (a mutation-agent failure mode), not an equivalent mutant.

answer.text: Is a test that is non-deterministic across CI runs

feedback.text: That is a flaky test, a test-agent failure mode, not an equivalent mutant.

generalfeedback.text: An equivalent mutant is semantically identical to the original: it produces the same behaviour on every input, so no test can distinguish it — it is uncatchable. The equivalence agent exists to identify and remove such mutants.

questiontext.text: Which agent decides whether a mutant is equivalent?

answer.text: The equivalence agent (Agent 2)

feedback.text: Correct — it is the LLM-as-judge for equivalence.

answer.text: The mutation agent (Agent 1)

feedback.text: Agent 1 generates mutants; it does not judge them.

answer.text: The test agent (Agent 3)

feedback.text: Agent 3 writes the killing test; equivalence has already been decided before it runs.

answer.text: The CI system

feedback.text: CI runs the generated tests; it does not judge mutant equivalence.

generalfeedback.text: The equivalence agent (Agent 2) is the LLM-as-judge that decides whether a given mutant is equivalent to the original.

questiontext.text: Which agent generates the mutants?

questiontext.text: Compared with the rule-based baseline, the LLM-guided approach is described as:

answer.text: Domain- and issue-aware, whereas rule-based mutation is not

feedback.text: Correct — the LLM can target faults relevant to the domain and the issue at hand.

feedback.text: It is the LLM approach that is domain-aware; being domain-aware is its advantage, not a blindness.

feedback.text: Targeting specific fault classes is exactly what the LLM-guided approach does.

generalfeedback.text: The LLM-guided pipeline is domain- and issue-aware — it can target fault classes that matter for the code under test — while the rule-based baseline applies generic syntactic operators with no such awareness.

questiontext.text: The phrase "LLM-as-judge" in this pipeline refers to which agent's mode of operation?

feedback.text: Correct — it uses the LLM to judge equivalence.

answer.text: CI deciding whether a test is flaky

feedback.text: CI applies a quality gate, but "LLM-as-judge" names the equivalence agent.

generalfeedback.text: "LLM-as-judge" describes the equivalence agent (Agent 2), which uses the LLM to judge whether a mutant is equivalent to the original.

name.text: Which mutants reach the test agent

questiontext.text: Which mutants does the test agent try to kill?

answer.text: The non-equivalent mutants that survive the equivalence agent

feedback.text: Correct — only mutants that can actually be killed are handed to the test agent.

generalfeedback.text: The equivalence agent removes equivalent (uncatchable) mutants first, so the test agent only tries to kill the non-equivalent mutants that survive that screening.

answer.text: true

name.text: Data flow into the equivalence agent

questiontext.text: What does the equivalence agent receive as its input?

answer.text: The mutants produced by the mutation agent, to judge which are equivalent

feedback.text: Correct — it screens the mutation agent's output before the test agent runs.

name.text: Why the equivalence agent is needed

questiontext.text: Why does the LLM-guided pipeline need a dedicated equivalence agent, when a simpler rule-based flow might not?

answer.text: The LLM mutation agent produces a higher rate of equivalent mutants (~25%), so they must be filtered out

feedback.text: Correct — more equivalent mutants means a dedicated judge is worth the cost.

answer.text: The LLM never produces equivalent mutants, so the agent double-checks

feedback.text: The opposite is true: the LLM produces more equivalent mutants than the rule-based baseline.

answer.text: Because rule-based mutation cannot compile its mutants

feedback.text: The reason is the LLM's higher equivalent-mutant rate, not a compilation issue with rule-based mutation.

answer.text: To increase the number of equivalent mutants on purpose

feedback.text: The agent removes equivalent mutants; it does not create more.

generalfeedback.text: Because the LLM-guided mutation agent produces a higher equivalent-mutant rate (~25%, versus roughly 10–15% for rule-based mutation), the pipeline adds an equivalence agent to filter those uncatchable mutants out before the expensive test-generation step.

questiontext.text: How do the reported mutant kill rates compare between the rule-based baseline and the LLM-guided pipeline?

answer.text: Rule-based ~2.4% vs LLM-guided ~15%

feedback.text: Correct — the LLM-guided approach kills a far larger share of mutants.

answer.text: Rule-based ~15% vs LLM-guided ~2.4%

feedback.text: The figures are reversed: LLM-guided is the higher one, at ~15%.

answer.text: Both about 25%

feedback.text: 25% is the LLM's equivalent-mutant rate, not the kill rate.

answer.text: Both close to 100%

feedback.text: Neither approach reaches anywhere near 100%; the reported kill rates are 2.4% and 15%.

generalfeedback.text: The rule-based baseline kills about 2.4% of mutants, while the LLM-guided pipeline kills about 15% — a large jump attributed to targeting specific fault classes.

questiontext.text: A generated test passes and fails non-deterministically across CI runs and is rejected. Which agent's failure mode is this?

answer.text: The test agent — it produced a flaky (non-deterministic) test

feedback.text: Correct — flaky tests are a test-agent failure mode, caught by the CI quality gate.

answer.text: The mutation agent — it produced an equivalent mutant

feedback.text: Flakiness is about the test's determinism, not about the mutant.

answer.text: The equivalence agent — it misjudged equivalence

feedback.text: A misjudged equivalence is a different symptom; flakiness is a property of the generated test.

answer.text: CI — it introduced randomness into the test

feedback.text: CI detects and rejects the flaky test; the test agent generated it.

generalfeedback.text: Generating a flaky (non-deterministic) test that CI rejects is a failure mode of the test agent. A quality gate filters such tests out.

questiontext.text: A produced mutant is syntactically invalid and fails to build. Which agent's failure mode is this?

answer.text: The mutation agent — it emitted syntactically invalid code

feedback.text: Correct — emitting invalid, non-building code is a mutation-agent failure mode.

answer.text: The test agent — it wrote a flaky test

feedback.text: Flakiness is a test-agent issue; this is a mutant that fails to build.

answer.text: The equivalence agent — it marked a mutant equivalent by mistake

feedback.text: That is a different failure; here the mutant itself does not compile.

answer.text: The engineer — they rejected the test

feedback.text: The problem is invalid mutant code, produced by the mutation agent.

generalfeedback.text: Emitting syntactically invalid code that fails to build is a failure mode of the mutation agent (Agent 1); such mutants are discarded.

questiontext.text: The equivalence agent adds a preprocessing step that strips comments before judging. Why?

answer.text: Comment differences caused about 25% of its false positives, so removing them improves accuracy

feedback.text: Correct — comment diffs were a large source of false positives, fixed by stripping comments.

answer.text: Comments make the code compile faster

feedback.text: The reason is judging accuracy, not compile speed.

answer.text: Comments are needed by the test agent, so they are moved aside

feedback.text: They are stripped to help the equivalence judge, not relocated for the test agent.

answer.text: Stripping comments increases the equivalent-mutant rate on purpose

feedback.text: It improves the judge's precision and recall; it is not about inflating equivalence.

generalfeedback.text: Comment differences accounted for roughly 25% of the equivalence agent's false positives. Stripping comments as a preprocessing step removes that noise and lifts precision and recall (from 0.79/0.47 to about 0.95/0.96).

questiontext.text: How does the equivalent-mutant rate of the LLM-guided approach compare with the rule-based baseline?

answer.text: Higher for the LLM (~25%) than rule-based (~10–15%)

feedback.text: Correct — the LLM produces more equivalent mutants, motivating the equivalence agent.

answer.text: Lower for the LLM (~5%) than rule-based (~25%)

answer.text: Zero for the LLM

feedback.text: The LLM's equivalent-mutant rate is about 25%, not zero.

generalfeedback.text: The LLM-guided approach has a higher equivalent-mutant rate (~25%) than the rule-based baseline (~10–15%) — a cost of targeting specific fault classes, which is why a dedicated equivalence judge is needed.

questiontext.text: A generated test fails on BOTH the original program and the mutant. Which agent's failure mode is this, most directly?

answer.text: The test agent — it produced a test with a build or logic error, not a valid mutation-killing test

answer.text: CI — it ran the test in the wrong order

generalfeedback.text: A test that fails on both the original and the mutant is not distinguishing them — it has a build or logic error. That is a test-agent failure mode; a valid killing test must pass on the original and fail on the mutant.

questiontext.text: What is credited with the LLM-guided pipeline's much higher kill rate?

answer.text: Because the test agent can produce flaky or otherwise invalid tests that must be filtered out

generalfeedback.text: Because the LLM-guided mutation agent targets specific fault classes, it kills more mutants (~15% vs ~2.4%) but also generates more equivalent ones (~25% vs ~10–15%). questiontext.text: Why does the coverage-blind, rule-based baseline achieve only ~2.4% kill rate compared with the LLM's ~15%?

answer.text: It applies generic syntactic operators without domain or issue awareness, so it rarely targets the fault classes that matter

feedback.text: Correct — without domain/issue awareness it cannot aim at meaningful faults.

name.text: Symptom: test fails on original and mutant

questiontext.text: Symptom: a generated test fails on the original program as well as on the mutant. Which agent's failure best explains this, and why?

answer.text: The test agent — a valid killing test must pass on the original and fail on the mutant; failing on both means a build/logic error in the test

feedback.text: Correct — the test cannot be distinguishing anything if it also fails on the original.

answer.text: The equivalence agent — it should have caught this as equivalent

feedback.text: Equivalence would make the test pass on both, not fail on both; the fault is in the test.

answer.text: The mutation agent — the mutant is invalid

answer.text: CI — it mislabelled a passing test as failing

generalfeedback.text: A correct mutation-killing test passes on the original and fails on the mutant. Failing on both means the test itself is broken (build or logic error) — a test-agent failure mode, distinct from an equivalent mutant (passes on both) or an invalid mutant (won't build).

feedback.text: The equivalence agent judges; it does not produce malformed mutants.

answer.text: CI — the build environment is misconfigured

feedback.text: The malformed mutant is generated by the mutation agent, independent of CI setup.

generalfeedback.text: A mutant that is syntactically invalid and fails to build is a mutation-agent failure mode. Such mutants are discarded before the rest of the pipeline runs.

name.text: Symptom: uncatchable mutant wastes the test agent

questiontext.text: Symptom: the test agent repeatedly fails to kill one particular mutant no matter what test it writes, and analysis shows the mutant is behaviourally identical to the original. Which agent should have prevented this?

answer.text: The equivalence agent — it should have judged this mutant equivalent and removed it

feedback.text: Correct — an uncatchable mutant reaching the test agent is a missed-equivalence (recall) failure.

answer.text: The test agent — it just needs a better test

feedback.text: No test can kill an equivalent mutant; the fix is to filter it, which is the judge's job.

answer.text: The mutation agent — it should not generate any equivalent mutants

feedback.text: The LLM inevitably produces some (~25%); the equivalence agent exists precisely to catch them.

answer.text: CI — it should have skipped the mutant

feedback.text: CI runs tests; deciding equivalence is the equivalence agent's role.

generalfeedback.text: A behaviourally-identical (equivalent) mutant can never be killed. If it reaches the test agent, the equivalence agent missed it — a recall failure. This is exactly the waste the equivalence agent (with comment-stripping preprocessing lifting recall to ~0.96) is meant to prevent.

name.text: Why kill rate alone is insufficient

questiontext.text: Why does the pipeline report engineer acceptance rather than relying on kill rate alone?

answer.text: A test can kill a mutant yet still be flaky, hard to read, or otherwise unwanted, so engineer acceptance measures real-world value

feedback.text: Correct — killing a mutant does not guarantee a test engineers will actually keep.

answer.text: Kill rate cannot be measured for LLM-generated tests

feedback.text: Kill rate is measured (2.4% vs 15%); acceptance is an additional, complementary metric.

answer.text: Engineer acceptance is identical to the kill rate

feedback.text: They are different metrics; acceptance captures value the kill rate misses.

answer.text: Acceptance replaces the need for an equivalence agent

feedback.text: Acceptance is an outcome metric; the equivalence agent addresses a different problem.

generalfeedback.text: A high kill rate does not mean a test is one engineers will adopt: it may be flaky, unreadable, or low-value. Reporting engineer acceptance captures whether the generated tests deliver real, kept-in-the-suite value, not just mutant kills.

name.text: Why filter flaky and invalid outputs

questiontext.text: Why is a filtering/acceptance gate essential given the test agent's and mutation agent's failure modes?

answer.text: Without gates, flaky tests and tests that fail on both versions (and invalid mutants) would pollute the suite, so they must be filtered before acceptance

feedback.text: Correct — gates keep unreliable and broken outputs out of the delivered suite.

answer.text: Gates increase the equivalent-mutant rate to make the judge's job easier

feedback.text: Gates filter bad outputs; they do not manipulate the equivalent-mutant rate.

answer.text: Gates let the pipeline skip the equivalence agent

feedback.text: The equivalence agent remains; gates handle a separate problem (bad tests and mutants).

answer.text: Gates convert equivalent mutants into killable ones

feedback.text: Nothing can make an equivalent mutant killable; gates only filter outputs.

generalfeedback.text: The mutation agent can emit invalid mutants, and the test agent can emit flaky tests or tests that fail on both original and mutant. A filtering/acceptance gate keeps these unreliable or broken artifacts out of the final suite, so only valid, deterministic mutation-killing tests are accepted.

name.text: Net effect of preprocessing on the flow

questiontext.text: After comment stripping raises the equivalence agent to ~0.95 precision / ~0.96 recall, what is the net effect on the downstream test agent?

answer.text: Fewer equivalent mutants slip through and fewer killable mutants are wrongly dropped, so the test agent spends its effort on genuinely killable mutants

feedback.text: Correct — high precision and recall together mean the test agent gets a cleaner, catchable input set.

answer.text: The test agent now also has to judge equivalence itself

feedback.text: Judging stays with the equivalence agent; preprocessing just makes its output cleaner.

answer.text: The mutation agent stops producing equivalent mutants

feedback.text: The mutation agent still produces ~25% equivalents; the judge just filters them better.

answer.text: The kill rate drops below the rule-based 2.4%

feedback.text: Better filtering does not lower the kill rate; it focuses the test agent on catchable mutants.

generalfeedback.text: High recall (~0.96) means few equivalent mutants slip through to waste the test agent; high precision (~0.95) means few catchable mutants are wrongly discarded. Together they give the test agent a clean set of genuinely killable mutants to target.

name.text: Cost accepted for a higher kill rate

questiontext.text: The pipeline accepts a higher equivalent-mutant rate (~25%) as a deliberate cost. What does it buy, and how is the cost contained?

answer.text: It buys a much higher kill rate (~15% vs ~2.4%) by targeting fault classes; the cost is contained by the equivalence agent that filters the extra equivalents

feedback.text: Correct — the equivalence judge is the containment mechanism for the extra equivalents.

answer.text: It buys faster builds; the cost is contained by CI

feedback.text: The payoff is a higher kill rate, and the containment is the equivalence agent, not build speed.

answer.text: It buys fewer mutants overall; the cost is contained by the test agent

feedback.text: The gain is kill rate from fault-class targeting; equivalents are contained by the judge.

answer.text: It buys nothing; the extra equivalents are pure loss

feedback.text: They are the price of the ~15% kill rate, and the equivalence agent limits their downstream cost.

generalfeedback.text: Targeting specific fault classes lifts the kill rate to ~15% but raises the equivalent-mutant rate to ~25%. The equivalence agent (with comment-stripping preprocessing) contains that cost by filtering the extra equivalent mutants before the test agent runs.

questiontext.text: Two symptoms: (A) a test passes on both the original and the mutant; (B) a test fails on both. Which diagnosis is correct?

answer.text: A points to an equivalent (or unkilled) mutant, an equivalence-agent concern; B points to a broken test, a test-agent concern

feedback.text: Correct — passing on both means no distinction (equivalence); failing on both means the test is broken.

answer.text: Both A and B mean the test agent wrote a flaky test

feedback.text: Flakiness is non-determinism across runs; neither A nor B is about run-to-run variance.

answer.text: Both A and B mean the mutant failed to build

feedback.text: A mutant that fails to build would not run at all; in both A and B a test executes.

answer.text: A means a broken test; B means an equivalent mutant

feedback.text: This reverses the two: passing on both is the equivalence signal, failing on both is the broken-test signal.

generalfeedback.text: Passing on both original and mutant (A) means the test cannot distinguish them — the mutant is equivalent or simply unkilled, an equivalence-agent concern. Failing on both (B) means the test is broken (build/logic error) — a test-agent concern. The two symptoms map to different agents.

questiontext.text: Why is equivalence judging placed before, rather than after, test generation?

answer.text: So the expensive test agent is never asked to kill uncatchable mutants, saving effort on equivalents that no test could kill

feedback.text: Correct — screening first avoids wasted test-generation work.

answer.text: So the equivalence agent can read the generated tests

feedback.text: It judges mutants, not tests, and runs before test generation.

answer.text: Because equivalence can only be judged once a killing test exists

feedback.text: Equivalence is a property of the mutant vs the original, independent of any generated test.

answer.text: To raise the equivalent-mutant rate before testing

feedback.text: Ordering does not change the rate; it avoids wasting the test agent on equivalents.

generalfeedback.text: Test generation is the expensive step. Filtering equivalent mutants first means the test agent is never asked to kill a mutant that no test could ever kill, so the pipeline spends its costly effort only on genuinely catchable mutants.

name.text: Consequence of disabling the equivalence agent

questiontext.text: A team disables the equivalence agent to save a step. Given the LLM mutation agent's ~25% equivalent-mutant rate, what is the most likely consequence?

answer.text: Roughly a quarter of mutants reaching the test agent are uncatchable, so it wastes effort trying to kill mutants no test can ever kill

feedback.text: Correct — with ~25% equivalents unfiltered, much test-agent effort is spent on uncatchable mutants.

answer.text: The kill rate rises above 15% because more mutants are attempted

feedback.text: Attempting equivalent mutants cannot kill them, so the kill rate does not improve.

answer.text: The mutation agent stops producing equivalent mutants

feedback.text: The mutation agent's ~25% equivalent rate is unchanged; only the filter is gone.

answer.text: Flaky tests are eliminated

feedback.text: Flakiness is a separate test-agent quality-gate issue, unaffected by removing the equivalence judge.

generalfeedback.text: Without the equivalence agent, the ~25% of mutants that are equivalent flow straight to the test agent, which then wastes effort on mutants that no test can kill. That wasted work is exactly what the equivalence agent (with comment-stripping preprocessing) is there to prevent.
